learningObjectives.title: Medieval monarchy and challenges to power
The struggle between Crown and Parliament

questions.q: Which king was forced to seal Magna Carta in 1215?
questions.explain: King John sealed Magna Carta in 1215 after his barons rebelled against his misrule and heavy taxation.

questions.q: In which year was Magna Carta sealed?
questions.explain: Magna Carta was sealed by King John at Runnymede in 1215.

questions.q: Which principle did Magna Carta help to establish?
options: The king was subject to the law
Only Parliament could rule the country
Peasants were given the right to vote
questions.explain: Magna Carta established that even the monarch had to obey the law and could not act entirely as he wished.

questions.q: Why was Simon de Montfort's parliament of 1265 significant?
options: It included ordinary townsmen and knights, not just barons
It gave women the right to vote
questions.explain: For the first time knights of the shires and burgesses from towns were summoned, widening who was represented.

questions.q: In which year did the Peasants' Revolt take place?
questions.explain: The Peasants' Revolt broke out in 1381 during the reign of Richard II.

questions.q: What was a major cause of the Peasants' Revolt?
questions.explain: Anger at a series of Poll Taxes, which fell equally on rich and poor, was a key trigger of the revolt.

questions.q: In 1381 a group of peasants led by Wat Tyler marched on London to protest against taxation and demand better conditions. This event is known as:
questions.explain: The 1381 rising led by Wat Tyler against the Poll Tax is known as the Peasants' Revolt.

questions.q: In which year did the English Civil War begin?
questions.explain: Fighting between Charles I and Parliament broke out in 1642.

questions.q: Which monarch was executed in 1649 after the Civil War?
questions.explain: Charles I was tried and executed in January 1649, an unprecedented act against a reigning king.

questions.q: Why did 'Ship Money' anger Parliament under Charles I?
options: It was a tax raised without Parliament's consent
It funded new schools for the poor
It was a tax that fell only on peasants
questions.explain: Charles extended Ship Money inland and levied it without Parliament, which many saw as illegal taxation.

questions.q: Who became 'Lord Protector' of England after the Civil War?
questions.explain: Oliver Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector during the republican Protectorate of the 1650s.

questions.q: In which year did the Glorious Revolution take place?
questions.explain: In 1688 James II was replaced by William and Mary in what became known as the Glorious Revolution.

questions.q: What was the main significance of the Bill of Rights (1689)?
options: It limited the monarch's power and increased Parliament's authority
It gave all men the right to vote
It made the monarch head of the Church
questions.explain: The Bill of Rights restricted royal power, requiring parliamentary consent for taxes and a standing army.

questions.q: When William and Mary took the throne in 1689, they had to accept that they could not raise taxes or keep an army without Parliament's agreement. Which document set out these limits?
questions.explain: The 1689 Bill of Rights placed these conditions on the new monarchs, confirming Parliament's authority.

questions.q: In which year was the Great Reform Act passed?
questions.explain: The Great Reform Act was passed in 1832, beginning the modern reform of Parliament.

questions.q: What was one effect of the Great Reform Act 1832?
options: It abolished some 'rotten boroughs' and gave the vote to more middle-class men
It gave all women the vote
It gave every adult the right to vote
questions.explain: The Act redistributed seats away from 'rotten boroughs' and extended the franchise to more property-owning middle-class men.

questions.q: Which was one of the six demands of the Chartists?
questions.explain: The People's Charter's six points included a secret ballot, alongside votes for all men and payment of MPs.

questions.q: How did the suffragettes differ from the suffragists?
options: Suffragettes used militant, direct action while suffragists campaigned peacefully
Suffragettes campaigned peacefully while suffragists used violence
Both groups refused to campaign at all
Suffragettes wanted votes only for men
questions.explain: The suffragettes (WSPU) used militant tactics, whereas the suffragists (NUWSS) preferred peaceful, constitutional methods.

questions.q: In 1918 the Representation of the People Act was passed. Would a 25-year-old woman have been able to vote under this Act?
options: No, because women could only vote from age 30 (with a property qualification)
Yes, all women over 21 could vote
No, women could not vote at all
Yes, all adults over 18 could vote
questions.explain: The 1918 Act gave the vote to women over 30 who met a property qualification, so a woman of 25 could not yet vote.

questions.q: A woman aged 21 votes for the first time in a general election on the same terms as men. Which 1928 law made this possible?
questions.explain: The Equal Franchise Act of 1928 gave women the vote at 21 on the same terms as men.
